subject: AI & Agents
title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Grounding AI in Facts
description: Learn Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Grounding AI in Facts in one minute.

hook.text: What if the AI could look up facts before answering instead of relying on memory? That's RAG.

buildup.text: RAG retrieves relevant documents from a database and feeds them to the LLM as context.

discovery.text: This grounds responses in actual sources, dramatically reducing hallucinations on factual questions.

twist.text: The retrieval step can fail — pulling irrelevant documents leads to confidently wrong answers anyway.

climax.text: RAG has become the standard architecture for enterprise AI chatbots that need reliable information.

punchline.text: Don't trust your memory. Look it up. Good advice for humans and AI.

quiz.question: How does RAG reduce AI hallucinations?
options: It retrieves relevant documents to ground answers in actual sources
It prevents the model from generating any text
It makes the model smaller and faster

details.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation fetches relevant documents from a knowledge base and includes them in the prompt, grounding the LLM's response in real, up-to-date information rather than relying on memory alone.
details.whyItMatters: RAG solves two critical LLM problems: outdated knowledge and hallucination. By providing source documents, it enables accurate, verifiable answers grounded in authoritative information.
takeaways: RAG retrieves relevant documents and adds them to the prompt
It reduces hallucinations by grounding responses in source material
It keeps LLM knowledge current without expensive retraining

faq.question: How does RAG work in practice?
faq.answer: When a user asks a question, the system searches a knowledge base for relevant documents using embeddings. The retrieved documents are added to the LLM prompt, and the model generates an answer based on that context.

faq.question: When should you use RAG instead of fine-tuning?
faq.answer: Use RAG when information changes frequently, when source attribution matters, or when you need answers from specific documents. Use fine-tuning when you want to change the model's overall behavior or writing style.
